readingInstruction: Read Acts 9:1-43. Saul meets the risen Christ on the Damascus road, is converted, and begins to preach. Peter heals Aeneas and raises Tabitha. Notice how Jesus identifies himself with his people.
settingTheScene: Saul of Tarsus, a Pharisee trained under Gamaliel, was the leading persecutor of the church. He obtained letters from the high priest to arrest believers in Damascus. This is the pivotal conversion in Acts. Luke tells it here, and Paul tells it again in chapters 22 and 26. It changed the history of the church. The persecutor became the apostle to the Gentiles.
observation: “But Saul, still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest” (9:1).
“Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (9:4).
“Who are you, Lord? And he said, I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting” (9:5).
“Go, for he is a chosen instrument of mine to carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel” (9:15).
“For I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name” (9:16).
“And immediately he proclaimed Jesus in the synagogues, saying, He is the Son of God” (9:20).
“So the church throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace and was being built up” (9:31).
interpretation:
Saul is on the road to Damascus when a light from heaven flashes around him. He falls to the ground and hears a voice: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” Notice that Jesus says “me.” To persecute the church is to persecute Christ. The church is united to him as a body to its head. “Who are you, Lord?” “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.” Saul has been convinced that Jesus was a blasphemer who died under God’s curse. Now he meets him, glorified.

Saul is blind and led by the hand into Damascus. For three days he neither eats nor drinks. A disciple named Ananias is told in a vision to go to him. Ananias protests: this man has done great harm to your saints. But the Lord says, “Go, for he is a chosen instrument of mine to carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel. For I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name.” Ananias goes, lays hands on him, and calls him “Brother Saul.” Something like scales fall from his eyes, and he is baptized.

His conversion is the work of sovereign grace. He was not seeking Christ. He was breathing threats. Jesus found him. And his call was clear from the start: to carry Christ’s name to the Gentiles. Immediately he proclaims Jesus in the synagogues: “He is the Son of God.” The people are amazed. “Is this not the man who made havoc in Jerusalem?” He baffles the Jews by proving that Jesus is the Christ. The Jews plot to kill him, and the disciples let him down over the wall in a basket.

In Jerusalem, the disciples are afraid of him, but Barnabas takes him and brings him to the apostles. Barnabas, the encourager, is vital here. Luke notes that the church throughout Judea, Galilee, and Samaria had peace, was built up, and multiplied.

Peter heals Aeneas, a paralytic in Lydda, and raises Tabitha (Dorcas), a woman known for good works, in Joppa. Many believe. Peter stays in Joppa with Simon, a tanner, a detail that prepares for the next chapter, because tanners were ceremonially unclean.
connection: Galatians 1:11-24 is Paul’s own account of his conversion. Philippians 3:4-11 tells how he counted all things as loss. 1 Timothy 1:12-16 says Christ came to save sinners, of whom Paul is the foremost. Ephesians 5:30 says we are members of his body. Matthew 25:40 and 25:45 speak of what is done to the least of these. 2 Corinthians 11:23-33 recounts his sufferings, including the basket. Romans 15:15-21 shows his Gentile mission.
application:
Remember your own conversion, however quiet. Write down how Christ found you.

Be an Ananias to someone who seems beyond reach. Is there someone you’ve written off?

Be a Barnabas: look for someone to encourage and bring into the fellowship.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for finding you, like Saul on the road.
Thank him for being one with his people.
Ask him to use you as he used Saul.
